edits.definition: A regenerative economy is an economic framework in which production and consumption actively restore the natural systems they draw upon — replenishing soil, recharging groundwater, regrowing forests and biodiversity — so that nature ends each cycle healthier, not merely unharmed. It goes one step beyond sustainability: a sustainable economy limits its damage to zero, while a regenerative economy aims for a net-positive ecological balance, in the way regenerative farming rebuilds topsoil year after year rather than just preserving what is left.

Range is the difference between the maximum and minimum values of a data set — the distance from the smallest observation to the largest. It is the quickest measure of spread: if marks in a class run from 21 to 98, the range is 98 − 21 = 77. Its strength is simplicity; its weakness is that it depends on just two values, so one extreme score can inflate it wildly even when the rest of the data sits close together.

Levels of organisation refer to the hierarchy of structure in living things, in which each level is built from the one below it. The cell is the basic building block; similar cells doing one job group into a tissue; different tissues combine into an organ such as the stomach; organs working together form an organ system such as the digestive system; and all the systems together make the complete organism. Each step up brings new abilities — a heart can pump, but a single muscle cell cannot — which is why life works only when every level plays its part.

In a rhombus, the two diagonals intersect at right angles and each diagonal divides the other into two equal segments — in other words, the diagonals are perpendicular bisectors of each other. This property follows from the rhombus's four equal sides and produces its most useful consequence: the diagonals split a rhombus into four congruent right triangles, so the area can be found as half the product of the diagonals, d₁ × d₂ ÷ 2 — no side length or height required.

Rights are the freedoms and claims guaranteed to individuals so that they can live with dignity and develop their personality — legal in standing, social in reach and moral in force. In India they are written into the Constitution itself, in Part III (Articles 12–35), as the Fundamental Rights: equality, freedom of speech and expression, freedom of religion, protection against exploitation, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies. Because the Constitution guarantees them, no law or government action can ordinarily violate them — and any citizen may go to court to enforce them against the state itself.

Cities are the non-agricultural economic hubs of an economy: dense settlements where secondary activities (manufacturing, construction) and tertiary activities (services, commerce, finance, transport) concentrate and feed on each other's presence. Density makes specialisation possible — the doctor, the coder and the trucker each serve thousands — and specialisation creates agglomeration economies, the efficiency gains of having suppliers, workers and customers within reach of one another. It is this concentration, not their population alone, that lets cities generate employment and income out of proportion to the land they occupy.

Major world river systems — the Nile, Amazon, Ganga, Mississippi, Yangtze and their kind — are vast natural watercourses that gather water from thousands of tributaries and drain entire continental basins to the sea. Each is a shaper as well as a carrier: cutting valleys, depositing the fertile floodplains and deltas on which agriculture stands, and feeding wetlands that steady the local climate. Because they supply water, transport, fertile silt and fish in one channel, civilisations have clustered along them from Egypt to the Gangetic plain — the great rivers are where geography and history meet.

A hypothesis is a tentative, testable explanation or prediction — a reasoned guess about how things are or will be, proposed on the basis of earlier observations and existing knowledge. To be scientific, it must name a relationship between variables clearly enough that an experiment could prove it wrong: 'plants grow taller in red light than in green light' is a hypothesis; 'plants simply like some lights better' is not. An experiment then holds conditions controlled and lets the evidence speak — supporting the hypothesis, refuting it, or sending it back for revision.

A food web is the network of interconnected food chains in an ecosystem, drawn by linking each organism to everything it eats and to everything that eats it. Real ecosystems rarely run on a single chain — grass feeds deer and insects alike, and deer, insects and mice may all feed one predator — so the web gives a truer picture of how energy and nutrients flow along many alternative pathways. That interconnection is also nature's insurance: if one food source fails, the web reroutes the flow and keeps the ecosystem from collapsing with it.

Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth at every scale: the number of different species (species richness), the variety of genes within each species (genetic diversity, which lets populations resist disease and change), and the variety of ecosystems themselves — forests, wetlands, grasslands, reefs (ecosystem diversity). It is the measure of how richly stocked the living world is, from tigers and teak to soil bacteria. High biodiversity makes ecosystems stable and productive; when species vanish faster than they are replaced, the web that supplies our food, medicine and clean air frays thread by thread.

The production process is the systematic transformation of inputs into outputs: raw materials, labour, machines, energy and know-how go in, are combined and changed through a chosen technique, and emerge as goods and services that satisfy human wants and carry economic value. Wheat plus milling becomes flour; flour plus labour and an oven becomes bread; skill plus time becomes a haircut. Because wants are unlimited but resources are scarce, the heart of production is choosing — what to make, how much, and with which combination of inputs — so that scarce resources yield the greatest value.

Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) are the institutions of local self-government in India's towns and cities — municipal corporations, municipal councils and nagar panchayats — created and empowered under the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act (1992). They provide the public goods a dense settlement cannot do without: water supply, drainage, waste collection, street lighting, roads and public health. To pay for these they levy local taxes such as property tax and user charges, and they plan land use and licensing for the city. Elected by residents for five-year terms, they are the layer of democracy closest to urban daily life.
